cards.title: Climate Change Threatens Kiribati’s License-Rent Economy and Forces a Search for Post-Tuna State Capacity
cards.background: Kiribati is a Pacific island state of around 130,000 people whose economy depends heavily on tuna fishing access fees. Its Exclusive Economic Zone covers more than 3.4 million sq km, and the government says fishing licenses generated $137m in 2024, with licenses contributing to almost three-quarters of government income between 2018 and 2022. Scientists and regional bodies warn that warming Pacific waters are pushing tuna eastward, which could reduce foreign fleets’ demand for Kiribati licenses and hit both state revenue and local food supply.

prop_args.thesis: Climate-driven tuna migration will hollow out Kiribati’s fiscal base, so the state must urgently diversify away from a single ocean-rent model before revenue collapse becomes a sovereign crisis.
mechanisms: First, warming waters shift tuna stocks out of Kiribati’s EEZ, which directly destroys the rent the state collects from foreign fleets. This is because (1) tuna react to temperature changes of within a tenth of a degree Celsius, (2) studies cited in the article say migration will be eastwards away from many island states, and (3) if fleets can no longer reliably catch fish in Kiribati waters, they have less reason to buy licenses.

Second, the revenue shock is structurally dangerous because Kiribati is unusually dependent on this one source of income. Three reasons: one, licenses brought in $137m in 2024; two, they made up almost three-quarters of government income from 2018 to 2022; three, that is roughly two-fifths of GDP, so even a moderate decline becomes a macroeconomic shock rather than a sectoral problem.

Third, the loss of fishing income cascades into state fragility through food security and import dependence. This matters because (1) local catches are already expected to fall under both high- and low-emissions scenarios, (2) households will rely more on expensive imported food, and (3) outer islands that depend on fish for protein face both higher prices and worse nutrition, which increases welfare costs and political pressure on the government.

prop_args.thesis: Kiribati can use this climate shock as a forcing mechanism to build a more resilient economy, making adaptation and diversification more valuable than simply defending the status quo.
mechanisms: First, the crisis creates incentives for policy reform that were previously delayed by easy tuna rents. This is because (1) governments with concentrated resource income often underinvest in diversification, (2) the article says Kiribati is already expanding processing and canning rather than only selling licenses, and (3) it is also developing aquaculture and non-sea sectors like tourism, renewables, and an offshore sovereign wealth fund.

Second, international climate finance can partially offset the transition cost. Three reasons: one, the Green Climate Fund launched a $156.8m project across 14 Pacific countries and territories; two, it aims to improve warning systems and food security so states can anticipate tuna redistribution; three, it is expected to provide around four million nutritious fish meals each year for communities in Kiribati, reducing immediate welfare losses while reforms scale up.

Third, because Kiribati’s EEZ is enormous relative to its landmass, it still has strategic leverage in regional fisheries governance. This matters because (1) the country can negotiate access, processing, and monitoring arrangements, (2) it can monetize its ocean space through value-added activities rather than raw access fees alone, and (3) adaptation can preserve some revenue even if biomass shifts, so the outcome is not inevitable collapse.

opp_args.thesis: The bigger story is not state collapse but managed adaptation, because Kiribati still has policy tools, external support, and room to reprice its ocean economy.
mechanisms: First, the government is not passive; it is already diversifying and adding value. One, it is expanding tuna processing and canning domestically instead of only selling access; two, it is developing aquaculture such as milkfish, snapper, and sea cucumbers; three, it is seeking revenue from tourism, renewable energy, and an offshore sovereign wealth fund.

Second, the worst-case revenue loss is significant but not fatal, which limits the claim that climate change automatically breaks the economy. One, the ministry’s preliminary modelling says more than $10m in annual access-fee losses by 2050 under high emissions, but that is smaller than the current $137m annual license revenue base; two, the best-case low-emissions scenario predicts no decrease in tuna biomass in the EEZ; three, adaptation and emissions mitigation can therefore materially change the outcome.

Third, international support reduces the likelihood that climate change translates into immediate humanitarian or fiscal catastrophe. One, the $156.8m GCF project is specifically designed for tuna-dependent Pacific communities; two, it improves forecasting and food security, which helps the state plan around stock shifts; three, aid and technical assistance can bridge the transition while Kiribati builds alternative revenue streams.

cards.weighing: The biggest delta in this debate is whether climate change produces irreversible fiscal collapse or a painful but manageable transition. Prop wins if they show the license-rent model is so concentrated that even partial tuna migration creates sovereign stress; opp wins if they frame adaptation, aid, and diversification as enough to preserve state capacity and avoid a total revenue cliff.
motion_areas: TH, as a small island developing state, would prioritize climate adaptation over immediate economic diversification
